findings.where: Article specimen, the pull quote “Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on with a client country!”, at both widths
findings.fault: The pull quote is set in logo blue, the same colour as the link ('Streamlining the PPP Process…') a few lines below it and as the button. The tile's palette gives blue to the wordmark, links and the button. Here it is also used to emphasise ordinary text, so on this page blue no longer means only 'you can act on this'.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank reader skimming one of Mark's articles, who sees blue text as a link and tries to click the quote. The same goes for Angélique when she adds posts: she has no clear rule for when text may be blue.

findings.where: Type pair specimen against the rest of the tile: the motion sketch heading 'precise, light, quick', and the related-article title 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge' under the article
findings.fault: The tile states its own rule that Source Sans 3 is for 'the nav, buttons, labels and dates only' and that Gelasio is for display and reading. Two parts on the same page break that rule. A heading-sized principle line is set in semibold Source Sans in the quiet grey, and an article title is set in Source Sans, while the article title above it is in Gelasio. The same kinds of text are set two different ways, so the specimen contradicts the type roles it is meant to fix.
findings.who_objects: The layout and animation rounds that must 'draw inside one look' from this tile, and Angélique adding an article list. Each finds the tile showing two answers to whether a title or heading is serif or sans.

findings.where: Hero lede ('World Bank's'), the article title ('The World's Best…') and the Gelasio note ('Georgia's'), at both widths
findings.fault: Apostrophes look like straight typewriter ticks, but the same specimen uses curly quotation marks (“ ” and ‘Abundance’). Straight and curly marks are mixed in one setting.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of a lawyer-advisor's writing, and Mark himself. In a large serif headline the straight tick stands out as unfinished typesetting on a site whose whole look rests on its letterforms.
